description: I am a final year cs student at the university of Johannesburg.
summary:
PyroGrav turns NASA’s combustion research into an interactive fire safety dashboard. Researchers can rank investigations by relevance, compare measured flame spread with ML estimates in synchronized 3D simulations, and ask a research guide powered by NASA INDUS and DeepSeek to trace findings back to the original experiments.

I built separate ML models for flame spread along acrylic rods on Earth and aboard the International Space Station, and evaluated a third model for liquid droplet burning. In grouped development tests on 34 ISS observations, the ISS model reduced mean absolute error by 51% compared with using the nearest recorded observation.

PyroGrav also helps researchers decide what to test next. For one rod and airflow configuration, the guide found an exact Earth measurement and showed how the closest ISS tests differed. Researchers can use that evidence to plan a matched experiment and see where predictions, including those for lunar and Martian gravity, still need validation.
details:
I built PyroGrav around a practical question: if a material has been tested on Earth, what evidence tells us how it will burn aboard a spacecraft? The dashboard brings six NASA combustion study families into one searchable workbench. Researchers can rank investigations by relevance, compare experimental setups and measurements, and trace a result back to its original table or figure.

The 3D simulation connects what researchers see to what was measured. In the acrylic rod workbench, two synchronized chambers show how flame fronts advance along a rod over time. Researchers can compare a published spread rate with an ML estimate or a physics baseline and see the error in millimetres per second. The rate controls the front’s position, while flame shape and colour are illustrative. A second workbench explores how quickly liquid droplets burned in recorded FLEX experiments across different gas mixtures.

The ML results show when a model helps and when it can mislead. I trained separate flame-spread models for Earth and ISS conditions and evaluated them against a simple alternative: using the nearest recorded observation. Across 34 ISS observations in grouped development tests, the ISS-trained model reduced mean absolute error from 0.02152 to 0.01049 mm/s, a 51.3% reduction. The Earth-trained model performed worse than nearest lookup when applied to ISS data. Showing both outcomes helps researchers decide which estimates deserve weight.

The Space Guide helps turn those findings into a research decision. It combines NASA INDUS for research retrieval, DeepSeek for explanations, and read-only tools that query published records and saved model results. For example, a lookup for a 6.4 mm black acrylic rod at 18.5% oxygen and 2 cm/s airflow returned an Earth measurement of 0.059 mm/s. The reviewed ISS records contained nearby tests, but none matched all three conditions. The guide identified which conditions differed and flagged uncertainty in the units of those nearby measurements. That gives a researcher a specific comparison to investigate before proposing another burn.

I developed the dashboard with Next.js, TypeScript, and Three.js and used Python and PyTorch on an NVIDIA Blackwell GPU on my laptop for model training. The web app and INDUS retrieval run on Vercel, with DeepSeek hosted on Cloudflare. Throughout development, I kept published measurements, model estimates, and data-quality flags visible. PyroGrav’s intended impact is to help researchers find relevant evidence, recognize misleading comparisons, and choose better follow-up experiments. Lunar and Martian flame-spread predictions remain unvalidated.

View the source code, training scripts, and evaluation results on GitHub
